report:
Conclusion: “No” is too strong. For eligible heavy current/former smokers, regular low-dose CT (LDCT) screening is associated with lower lung-cancer mortality, though it does not remove risk and has harms.

The best evidence is randomized. The U.S. NLST enrolled 53,454 high-risk people and found LDCT reduced lung-cancer mortality versus chest X-ray; the commonly cited relative reduction was about 20%, with a smaller all-cause mortality reduction (https://www.sit-radiologie.fr/sites/www.sit-radiologie.fr/files/medias/documents/nlst_nejm_2011.pdf). The European NELSON trial then compared volume CT with no screening in high-risk current/former smokers and reported significantly lower lung-cancer mortality—about 24% in men and 33% in women at 10 years (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793).

Guidelines reflect this: USPSTF recommends annual LDCT for adults 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years who smoke or quit within 15 years, judging moderate certainty of moderate net benefit (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening). Cochrane is more cautious: annual LDCT is associated with reduced lung-cancer mortality in high-risk smokers, but cost-effectiveness and the balance of harms—false positives, invasive follow-up, overdiagnosis, radiation—still matter (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001991_screening-lung-cancer).

So: screening lowers the chance of dying from lung cancer for the right high-risk group; quitting smoking remains the larger risk reducer.
